02806 Social Data Analysis and Visualization - Project B¶

Group 3: s252711, s252692, s252611

link to the webpage: https://zoelinnn.github.io/

1. Motivation¶

1.1 What is your dataset?¶

Primary Dataset: DOB NOW Instead of BIS

NYC's Department of Buildings stores construction job filings in two parallel databases:

  • BIS (DOB Job Application Filings, ic3t-wcy2): Legacy system, operating since 2000 (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/DOB-Job-Application-Filings/ic3t-wcy2/about_data)
  • DOB NOW (Build Job Application Filings, w9ak-ipjd): New system, gradually rolled out since 2017 (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/DOB-NOW-Build-Job-Application-Filings/w9ak-ipjd/about_data)

We chose DOB NOW as our primary dataset for three reasons:

  • Currency: BIS has been declining since 2018 and was largely retired after 2022; DOB NOW is the system currently in active use, providing data through 2025.
  • Data quality: DOB NOW has standardized field names, is fully electronic, and has low missingness (key fields such as latitude and bbl have less than 3% missing).
  • Temporal alignment with PLUTO: PLUTO is a 2025 snapshot, and the DOB NOW time window aligns naturally with it, avoiding the "current PLUTO state vs. historical BIS filings" causal mismatch.

We considered merging the two datasets to obtain a longer time series but ultimately decided against it. The two systems have incompatible primary keys (numeric Job vs. prefixed job_filing_number), inconsistent date semantics (BIS's Pre-Filing Date is the submission date while DOB NOW's current_status_date is the most recent status update), entirely different Job Type encodings (NB/A1/A2 vs. ALT-CO/ALT-GC), and overlapping projects in the 2016–2019 transition period. Forcibly merging them would introduce serious specification inconsistencies — too costly for a two-week project.

Supplementary Dataset: PLUTO

We introduced PLUTO (Primary Land Use Tax Lot Output, 64uk-42ks) as an auxiliary dataset providing lot-level attributes (year built, FAR, owner type, etc.). (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Primary-Land-Use-Tax-Lot-Output-PLUTO-/64uk-42ks/about_data)

The two datasets are linked through BBL (Borough-Block-Lot, a 10-digit lot identifier), achieving a final match rate of 97.6%.

We retained only 11 PLUTO columns directly relevant to our analysis (yearbuilt, bldgclass, unitsres, unitstotal, numfloors, bldgarea, assesstot, builtfar, residfar, landmark, ownertype) to avoid column bloat.

1.2 Why did you choose this/these particular dataset(s)?¶

Together they form the minimal sufficient set for answering the question this project poses.

The value of permit filing data lies in its proximity to the moment of decision. Completed building data or property transaction records reflect outcomes that trail the original decision by years. Permit applications capture intention and action at the source, making them far more sensitive to shifts in market expectations and policy conditions. More importantly, they decompose the macro narrative of a construction surge into verifiable components, making the divergence between new buildings and alterations visible. If only total permit volume is examined, this structural change disappears entirely into the aggregate.

PLUTO is introduced to answer the second question: why does construction concentrate where it does rather than somewhere else. Permit data alone can describe where building is happening, but cannot explain why. Development potential, as a quantifiable variable, transforms the relationship between zoning capacity and market behavior into something testable rather than speculative.

Neither dataset is without limitation. PLUTO is a 2025 cross-sectional snapshot while the permit records span four years, meaning that a lot which received a filing in 2022 and completed construction by 2023 may show reduced remaining development potential in the 2025 snapshot precisely because that construction consumed floor area ratio. The analysis therefore describes spatial association rather than strict causality.

1.3 What was your goal for the end user's experience?¶

The project aims to dismantle a deeply held urban intuition. When most people think about construction in New York City, they picture the Manhattan skyline. The real surge is happening in Bushwick, Mott Haven, and Tottenville, names that carry none of the cultural weight of Midtown. Convincing readers to accept and genuinely internalize a conclusion that runs against their prior assumptions is the central narrative challenge this project had to solve.

Simply stating that Manhattan accounts for only 1.4 percent of new building filings is insufficient. A statistic can be acknowledged without being believed. The narrative structure is therefore designed as a progressive revelation: first establish credibility at the aggregate level by proving the surge is real and not a pandemic rebound, then narrow the lens to spatial distribution so readers can see on the map the contrast between Manhattan's near-blank panel and the deep red of the outer boroughs, and finally offer a lot-level mechanistic explanation that answers why.

The interactive maps and quarterly animation are designed so that readers discover the pattern themselves rather than being told it. People place more trust in conclusions they arrive at through active exploration than in those they receive passively. When a reader drags the timeline slider and watches Brooklyn and Staten Island deepen quarter by quarter while Manhattan remains pale throughout, the persuasive force of that visual experience cannot be replicated by a static chart.

The project ultimately aims to serve two audiences simultaneously. For urban planning practitioners and policy researchers, it offers a verifiable, lot-level spatial analysis framework. For ordinary New Yorkers, it offers a new lens through which to understand their own city: the neighborhoods genuinely reshaping New York's physical fabric over the coming decades are not the ones adjacent to Fifth Avenue, but the ones a few stops past the end of the L train.

2. Basic stats¶

2.1 Write about your choices in data cleaning and preprocessing.¶

2.1.1 Time window selection¶

Our time window went through three iterations:

Stage Window Reason
Initial 2010–2019 (BIS era) Default 10-year window from intuition
Revision 1 2003–2015 (based on BIS distribution) Discovered post-2016 data was actually a "system migration artifact"
Final 2021–2025 (DOB NOW) Recalibrated after switching to DOB NOW

2.1.2 Data clean and preprocess¶

DOB NOW provides 5 date fields, handled as follows:

  • filing_date: Primary time-axis variable for analysis (it marks the unambiguous start of the project lifecycle).
  • approved_date / first_permit_date / signoff_date: Used to derive process durations, but we do not drop rows based on their missingness — these missing values reflect the project's stage in the workflow (50% of projects haven't reached completion is normal), not data quality issues.
  • All dates were converted to pd.datetime, with invalid values (e.g., 0000-00-00) coerced to NaT.

Geographic Fields:

  • Coordinate filtering: lat ∈ [40.4, 41.0], lon ∈ [−74.3, −73.6] (NYC's reasonable bounds), removing out-of-range outliers.
  • Borough standardization: Uppercased and stripped of whitespace.
  • Retain NaN selectively: 6,403 records (0.7%) have a valid BBL but no coordinates. These were uniformly distributed across boroughs and years, suggesting random missingness. We exclude them from spatial analyses but keep them for non-spatial analyses.

Job Type Simplification: The original job_type field had numerous fine-grained values. We derived job_type_clean, simplified into 6 categories

  • NB ← New Building / ALT-CO with Existing Elements
  • ALT ← Alteration
  • ALT-CO ← Alteration CO
  • DM ← Full Demolition
  • NoWork ← No Work
  • Other ← Everything else

The simplification principle was to retain analytically meaningful core categories while preventing long-tail types from diluting the main analysis.

Filing Status Simplification: The original filing_status field contained 46 fine-grained values (e.g., On Hold – Pending Supersede of Owner, LL 158-2017-Denied, Plan Examiner Review), which was too fragmented for analysis. We derived filing_status_clean, semantically grouped into 6 categories:

  • Completed ← LOC Issued / CO Issued / Signed-off
  • Approved/Permitted ← Approved / Permit Entire / Permit Issued
  • In Review ← Plan Examiner Review / Pending / Awaiting / Incomplete
  • On Hold ← Various On Hold states
  • Terminated ← Withdrawn / Revoked / Denied / Intent to Revoke
  • Objections/Issues ← Objections / QA Failed The grouping criterion was semantic meaning, not frequency — for example, all "On Hold" states were merged into one category regardless of the specific reason for the hold.

PLUTO's Missingness: Two PLUTO fields had unusually high missingness (>65%), but this is by-design semantics rather than a data quality issue:

Field Missing Rate True Meaning
landmark_pluto 77.3% PLUTO populates this only for landmarked buildings; missing means "not landmarked"
ownertype_pluto 68.4% Populated only for non-private owners (City/Mixed/Tax-exempt); missing means "Private"

We addressed these with two derived fields:

  • is_landmark: Boolean, equivalent to landmark_pluto.notna().
  • ownertype_clean: Filled missing values with 'P' (Private) to make the field semantically complete.

Derived Fields: To support downstream analyses, we derived 8 additional fields:

  • Time-related (4 fields):
  • filing_year / filing_month / filing_quarter: For aggregations at different temporal granularities.
  • days_to_approval / days_to_signoff: Process durations through the approval workflow.
  • Project scale (3 fields):
  • units_added = proposed_dwelling_units − existing_dwelling_units
  • stories_added = proposed_no_of_stories − existing_stories
  • work_type_count: The number of work types involved in a project (sum of 12 binary work type indicators).
  • PLUTO-derived (2 fields):
  • development_potential = residfar_pluto − builtfar_pluto: The lot's "unreleased development potential," a key indicator for our spatial analysis.
  • building_era: Bins yearbuilt_pluto into 5 eras (Pre-1900, 1900–1945, 1945–1980, 1980–2010, 2010+).

2.2 Write a short section that discusses the dataset stats, containing key points/plots from your exploratory data analysis.¶

2.2.1 Dataset Overview¶

  • ~716,870 records of NYC construction job filings
  • Time window: April 2021 – December 2025 (In the first quarter of 2021, due to incomplete data from the system migration, it was excluded for our analysis)
  • 44 columns: 5 from PLUTO (lot attributes), the rest from DOB NOW (filing details) plus 8 derived fields
  • Geographic coverage: All 5 NYC boroughs, ~200 NTAs (Neighborhood Tabulation Areas)
  • PLUTO match rate: 97.6% (records successfully joined to lot-level attributes via BBL)

2.2.2 Key Distributions¶

Job Type Composition: The vast majority of filings are alterations to existing buildings, with new construction making up a small but rapidly growing share.

Job Type Share Description
ALT (Alteration) ~80% Standard renovations, system upgrades
ALT-CO (Alteration CO) ~7% Major alterations changing certificate of occupancy
NB (New Building) ~6% Ground-up new construction
NoWork ~5% Filings with no actual construction work
DM (Full Demolition) ~1% Full building demolitions (data starts 2023-04)
Other <1% Miscellaneous

Borough Distribution: Filings are unevenly distributed across boroughs, broadly tracking population and built density, Manhattan and Brooklyn together account for over half of all filings. The low rate of terminated or objected filings (~5% combined) suggests that most NYC construction applications proceed smoothly through the DOB system.

Borough Filings Share
Manhattan ~244,000 27.4%
Brooklyn ~234,000 26.3%
Queens ~177,000 19.9%
Bronx ~88,000 9.9%
Staten Island ~46,000 5.2%

Project Status: Filings reflect different stages of the DOB workflow at the time of data extraction.

Status (Cleaned) Share
Approved / Permitted ~45%
Completed ~40%
Objections / Issues ~3%
Terminated ~2%
On Hold ~1%
In Review / Other ~9%

2.2.3 Temporal Trends¶

  • Total filings are stable: Across 2021–2025, the total number of monthly filings hovers around 11,000–13,000, growing only modestly overall.
  • But composition is shifting dramatically: When broken out by Job Type, the picture changes:
  • ALT (the dominant category) grew only 5% from 2021 H2 to 2025
  • ALT-CO grew +253%
  • NB grew +258% — the largest absolute increase, from ~410 filings/month in 2021 H2 to ~1,470 filings/month in 2025

This dichotomy — stable total volume masking a structural shift toward new construction — frames the central question of our analysis.

The figure above shows the annual trend in NB (New Building) applications. For comparison, we have highlighted 2020 (the COVID period) and marked the 2019 baseline and the 2015 peak. It can be seen that new construction activity in NYC has been declining throughout the latter half of the 2010s. Then, by 2025—13,340 applications. This represents a 204% increase compared to pre-pandemic levels and is 56% higher than the 2015 peak. This is not merely a post-pandemic rebound. It is a genuine recovery in new construction that has surpassed historical levels.

3.2 Monthly trend by job type¶

In [ ]:
types_to_plot = ['ALT', 'NB', 'ALT-CO']

monthly = (df.groupby([pd.Grouper(key='filing_date', freq='ME'),
                       'job_type_clean'])
             .size()
             .unstack(fill_value=0))
monthly_smooth = monthly.rolling(window=3, center=True).mean()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 5), sharex=True)

for ax, jt in zip(axes, types_to_plot):
    ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly[jt], color=COLOR_PALETTE.get(jt, '#999'),
            alpha=0.35, linewidth=1, label='Monthly')
    ax.plot(monthly_smooth.index, monthly_smooth[jt],
            color=COLOR_PALETTE.get(jt, '#999'),
            linewidth=2.5, label='3-month rolling avg')
    ax.fill_between(monthly_smooth.index, 0, monthly_smooth[jt],
                    color=COLOR_PALETTE.get(jt, '#999'), alpha=0.15)

    avg_start = monthly[jt].loc['2021-07':'2021-12'].mean()
    avg_end = monthly[jt].loc['2025-01':'2025-12'].mean()
    change = (avg_end / avg_start - 1) * 100 if avg_start > 0 else 0

    ax.text(0.02, 0.95,
            f'2021 H2 avg: {avg_start:.0f}/mo\n'
            f'2025 avg: {avg_end:.0f}/mo\n'
            f'Change: +{change:.0f}%',
            transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=9, va='top',
            bbox=dict(boxstyle='round,pad=0.4',
                      facecolor='white', edgecolor='#ccc', alpha=0.9))

    ax.set_title(jt, fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_ylabel('Applications/month' if jt == 'ALT' else '')
    ax.set_xlabel('Month')
    ax.legend(loc='upper right', fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

fig.suptitle('Monthly Trend by Job Type, 2021-2025\n'
             '(comparing 2021 H2 to 2025 to avoid onboarding bias)',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Left (Alteration, ALT): Stable. Growth of just 5% over five years. There has been no increase in the workload for refurbishment workers.

Right (Alteration CO, ALT-CO): Rise. Applications to convert office buildings into residential properties and to repurpose retail spaces have increased by 253%.

Middle (New Building, NB): Rise. From 410 applications per month in the second half of 2021, the figure has surged to nearly 1,500 per month in 2025 – a 3.5-fold increase.

4. Genre¶

Which tools did you use from each of the 3 categories of Visual Narrative (Figure 7 in Segal and Heer). Why?¶

For Visual Structuring, we used Establishing Shot / Splash Screen, Consistent Visual Platform, and Progress Bar / Timebar. The opening of the website works like an establishing shot. It quickly tells readers what the project is about. After that, the website keeps a consistent layout, with repeated maps, charts, figure captions, and section titles. This makes the story easier to follow. The time-based figures also help readers see how the pattern changes from 2021 to 2025.

For Highlighting, we used Feature Distinction, Close-Ups, and Motion. We used color to separate job types and borough modes, and we used point size to show where NB activity is stronger. We also labeled important neighborhoods and used rankings to draw attention to the places driving the surge. The animated time views help show how NB activity changes over time.

For Transition Guidance, we used Object Continuity and Animated Transitions. The same ideas appear throughout the website: NB filings, borough modes, NTAs, and development potential. This helps readers connect one section to the next. The story first shows the citywide growth, then moves to boroughs and neighborhoods, and finally tests land development potential. The animations and repeated visual elements help the transitions feel natural.

Which tools did you use from each of the 3 categories of Narrative Structure (Figure 7 in Segal and Heer). Why?¶

For Ordering, we used Linear ordering. First, we show that the NB surge is real. Then we show where it happened. Finally, we ask whether land development potential helps explain the pattern. This order works well because readers need to understand the basic trend before they can understand the spatial explanation.

For Interactivity, we used Hover Highlighting / Details, Filtering / Selection / Search, and Very Limited Interactivity. The website lets readers hover over charts and maps to see more details about boroughs, NTAs, and neighborhoods. Some views also let readers compare patterns across time or categories. But we kept the interaction limited on purpose. We wanted the website to remain a guided story, not a complicated dashboard.

For Messaging, we used Captions / Headlines, Annotations, Introductory Text, and Summary / Synthesis. Each section has a clear title and a short explanation of what the reader should notice. The captions help explain the main takeaway from each figure. We also use careful language in the final section for summary.

5. Visualizations¶

5.1 Story 1: NYC is growing¶

Explain the visualizations you've chosen¶

In Story 1, we use the four figures from Section 3 (Data Analysis). They are all statistical analysis figures, progressing from a broad overview to borough-level patterns.

Why are they right for the story you want to tell?¶

1. Five-Year Application Total Overview¶

What it shows: A simple gray bar chart of total annual filings in NYC, 2021–2025.

Why it works: This figure does the unglamorous but essential work of setting up the puzzle. It tells the reader that NYC's overall construction activity has been remarkably stable. Non-technical readers expect "construction is growing" to mean "more total filings" — the flat-ish gray bars subtly contradict that expectation, creating narrative tension: if total construction isn't really increasing, then what is the story?

2. Three-Type Faceted Trend (NB / ALT / ALT-CO)¶

What it shows: Monthly filing trends for the three major Job Types, each with its own y-axis scale and clearly labeled growth rate (ALT: +5%, ALT-CO: +253%, NB: +258%).

Why it works:

  • Faceting over stacking: A stacked area chart would visually crush NB and ALT-CO under the dominant ALT. Separate panels with independent y-axes give the small-but-rapidly-growing categories equal visual weight.
  • Smoothed trend lines: Raw monthly data alone looks noisy; smoothed-only would lose authenticity. The combination preserves both signal and texture.
  • Embedded growth labels: Putting "+258%" directly on the NB panel turns the figure into a self-contained finding — a reader who only glances at it already knows the headline.
  • Distinguishes NB from ALT-CO: Despite similar growth rates, NB's higher absolute baseline (~410/month vs. ~302/month) and greater absolute change hint that it is the more substantial phenomenon — motivating our later focus on NB specifically.
3. 11-Year Long-Term Trend (2015–2025)¶

What it shows: A bar chart of NB filings per year from 2015 to 2025, combining BIS (legacy) and DOB NOW (current) data, with reference lines for the 2019 baseline and 2015 peak.

Why it works: By extending the timeline back to 2015, it reveals three findings at once:

  1. NB activity was already declining through the late 2010s (8,567 in 2015 → 4,395 in 2019), well before the pandemic.
  2. The 2020 pandemic trough (2,938) was modest, not catastrophic — a rebound argument can explain at most a ~50% recovery.
  3. 2025's level (13,340) exceeds the 2019 baseline by 204% and the 2015 peak by 56% — NYC has reached an NB level with no precedent in the past decade.
4. Borough Composition¶

What it shows: A 100%-stacked bar chart, one bar per borough, showing the percentage breakdown of Job Types per borough, with NB and ALT-CO percentages annotated above each bar.

Why it works: This figure acts as the bridge to Story 2. Having established that NB growth is real and unprecedented, the natural next question is "Where is this happening?" The figure surfaces a counterintuitive finding: the five boroughs behave like three different cities. This reframing establishes the conceptual scaffolding for Story 2 — spatial heterogeneity is about what kind of construction each area does, not just how much.

5.2 Story 2: The places where NYC is really growing¶

Explain the visualizations you've chosen.¶

In story 2, we use Plotly with geodata and one bar chart.

Why are they right for the story you want to tell?¶

  • 'NB vs. ALT Side-by-Side Comparison' is a two NTA-level choropleth maps side by side — ALT density (blue, left) vs. NB density (red, right). So far, the reader knows where NB is concentrated. But a skeptic might still think: "Maybe NB just follows where all construction happens — outer boroughs simply have more activity overall." This figure refutes that. The two maps look almost like inverses: ALT clusters tightly in Manhattan and inner Brooklyn, while NB clusters in outer-borough corridors and Staten Island. Manhattan is dark blue on the left and nearly white on the right. NB is not a smaller version of ALT — it follows a fundamentally different spatial logic. This finding does two things at once: it confirms that NB activity is a phenomenon worth explaining on its own terms, and it sharpens the question driving Story 3 — what makes these specific places attractive for new building?

The progression mirrors the natural flow of inquiry: see the pattern → identify the places → watch them emerge → confirm they're distinctive. By the end, the reader is fully prepared for Story 3's question: why these places?

5.3 Story 3: Development potential explains the lot-level geography, but neighborhood context adds complexity¶

Explain the visualizations you've chosen¶

In story 3, we used time-series charts to show how New Building (NB) filings changed from 2021 to 2025. These charts make the overall increase easy to see.

Then, we used maps to show where the growth happened. This is important because our story is not only about growth over time, but also about where that growth is located.

We also used stacked charts and borough comparisons to show that different parts of NYC have different construction patterns. For example, Manhattan is more renovation-heavy, while outer-borough neighborhoods show stronger NB activity.

Finally, we used scatterplots to connect NB activity with land development potential. These plots help show whether places with more room to build also have more NB filings.

Borough-mode internal comparison checks whether the development-potential pattern holds within Manhattan, the Outer Boroughs, and Staten Island. It strengthens the story by showing whether NB growth is only a borough-level pattern or also varies within each mode.

NTA centroid view is about spatial concentration. It shows where NB activity is located and helps readers connect the statistical pattern to actual areas of New York City.

6. Discussion¶

What went well?¶

The website works well as a guided story. It takes a large DOB dataset and turns it into a clear argument: NB filings increased sharply, the growth was not centered in Manhattan, and selected outer-borough neighborhoods became the main hotspots.

The visualizations also support the story well. Time-series charts show the growth, maps show where it happened, and scatterplots help connect NB activity to land development potential. The interaction is useful but not too complex, so readers can inspect details without getting lost.

What is still missing? What could be improved?, Why?¶

The main missing part is completion data. Filings and permits show administrative activity, but they do not prove that buildings were actually completed. So we should say “NB filing activity increased,” not “NYC built more new buildings.”

Another limitation is the PLUTO timing. Some land variables may come from a later snapshot, while filings happened between 2021 and 2025. This means the project shows spatial association, not causality.

A future version could add Certificate of Occupancy or completion records to connect filings to real built outcomes. The website could add short glossary boxes for terms like NB, ALT, NTA, FAR, and development potential, so non-technical readers can follow the story more easily.
